modules.summary: Module 1 develops the foundational capability of computing all six trigonometric ratios — sin A, cos A, tan A, cosec A, sec A, and cot A — for any acute angle A in a right triangle. Starting with real-world scenarios (Qutab Minar, river bank, hot-air balloon), Segment M1.S1 establishes the context for why such ratios are needed, formally defines all six ratios as fractions of the sides of right triangle ABC, and proves using AA similarity that these ratios are invariant under scaling. Segment M1.S2 extends this toolkit by showing how to recover all six ratios from a single given ratio, using the Pythagorean theorem to determine the missing side. The unifying mathematical insight across both segments is that trigonometric ratios capture the shape of a right triangle — the angle alone determines all six numbers, independent of the triangle's size. This module lays the groundwork for Module 2, where exact ratio values are derived for the standard angles 0°, 30°, 45°, 60°, and 90°.

topics.summary: Trigonometry is introduced as the branch of mathematics that studies relationships between the sides and angles of a triangle, with particular focus on right triangles. The procedure is to identify a physical situation involving a height, a base, and a line of sight, label the three sides of the resulting right triangle as opposite, adjacent, and hypotenuse relative to the angle of interest, and recognise that fixed ratios between these sides encode all measurable information about the angle. For example, in the Qutab Minar scenario, the ground from Priya to the base is the adjacent side, the minaret is the opposite side, and her line of sight is the hypotenuse, with her angle of elevation being angle A. This labelling convention is consistent throughout the chapter and is the prerequisite for defining trigonometric ratios in the next topic.
topics.topic_name: Introduction: Right Triangles in Real-Life Contexts
topics.brief_summary: Real-life situations such as the Qutab Minar and a wheelchair ramp are used to motivate right-triangle modelling, by identifying the opposite, adjacent, and hypotenuse sides relative to the relevant angle.
topics.modified_chunk:
HOOK: You have probably looked up at a tall building and wondered how architects measure its height without climbing it. Trigonometry is the mathematical tool that makes this possible — and by the end of this chapter, you will be using it yourself.

RECALL: In your earlier classes, you studied triangles, and in particular the right triangle — a triangle in which one angle is exactly 90°. The sides and angles of right triangles turn out to carry far more information than they might first appear.

CORE: There is perhaps nothing which so occupies the middle position of mathematics as trigonometry. – J.F. Herbart (1890)

Let us take some examples from our surroundings where right triangles can be imagined to be formed.

1. Suppose the students of a school are visiting Qutab Minar. Now, if a student is looking at the top of the Minar, a right triangle can be imagined to be made. Can the student find out the height of the Minar, without actually measuring it?

Think about this more carefully: Priya's class visits the Qutab Minar in Delhi. The ground from Priya to the Minar's base is one side of a right triangle, the Minar is the vertical side, and her line of sight to the top is the hypotenuse. Given one side and one angle, can we find the rest? This is the central question trigonometry answers.

2. Suppose a girl is sitting on the balcony of her house located on the bank of a river. She is looking down at a flower pot placed on a stair of a temple situated nearby on the other bank of the river. A right triangle is imagined to be made in this situation. If you know the height at which the person is sitting, can you find the width of the river?

3. Suppose a hot air balloon is flying in the air. A girl happens to spot the balloon in the sky and runs to her mother to tell her about it. Her mother rushes out of the house to look at the balloon. Now when the girl had spotted the balloon initially it was at point A. When both the mother and daughter came out to see it, it had already travelled to another point B. Can you find the altitude of B from the ground?

In all the situations given above, the distances or heights can be found by using some mathematical techniques, which come under a branch of mathematics called 'trigonometry'. The word 'trigonometry' is derived from the Greek words 'tri' (meaning three), 'gon' (meaning sides) and 'metron' (meaning measure). In fact, trigonometry is the study of relationships between the sides and angles of a triangle. The earliest known work on trigonometry was recorded in Egypt and Babylon. Early astronomers used it to find out the distances of the stars and planets from the Earth. Even today, most of the technologically advanced methods used in Engineering and Physical Sciences are based on trigonometrical concepts.

Similarly, when a carpenter builds a wheelchair-accessible ramp — vertical rise, horizontal base, slanted surface as hypotenuse — trigonometry provides the fixed relationships between the angle and the side lengths that are needed to cut the ramp to the correct dimensions.

In this chapter, we will study some ratios of the sides of a right triangle with respect to its acute angles, called trigonometric ratios of the angle. We will restrict our discussion to acute angles only. However, these ratios can be extended to other angles also. We will also define the trigonometric ratios for angles of measure 0° and 90°. We will calculate trigonometric ratios for some specific angles and establish some identities involving these ratios, called trigonometric identities.

CONVENTION NOTE — Variable conventions used throughout this chapter: We will label our standard right triangle as triangle ABC, right-angled at B. The angle under study will be angle A (or sometimes the Greek letter θ, theta, used interchangeably). The side opposite to angle A is BC; the side adjacent to angle A is AB; the hypotenuse is AC. These labels are consistent in every worked example and every proof in this chapter.

ERROR ALERT: Trigonometry is sometimes perceived as purely abstract. In fact, every situation where an angle connects two physical distances — a ramp and the ground, a line of sight and a building — is a trigonometric problem. The right triangle exists in the real world; mathematics gives us a precise way to describe it.

CHECK: Before moving on, pause and identify: in the Qutab Minar scenario, which physical feature corresponds to the opposite side, which to the adjacent side, and which to the hypotenuse, when angle A is Priya's angle of elevation?

In this chapter, we will study some ratios of the sides of a right triangle with respect to its acute angles, called trigonometric ratios of the angle. concept_bullets: A right triangle forms whenever a vertical height, a horizontal base, and a slanted line of sight meet — for example, the Qutab Minar (opposite), the ground (adjacent), and Priya's line of sight (hypotenuse) form exactly such a triangle.

The labels opposite, adjacent, and hypotenuse are always defined relative to the angle under study — if angle A is at Priya's position, BC (the side facing angle A) is the opposite side and AB is the adjacent side.

Trigonometric ratios are ratios of sides of a right triangle — for example, given a ramp with vertical rise 1 m and horizontal base 3 m, the ratio of rise to run is 1/3, which equals tan of the ramp angle.

Distances that cannot be measured directly can be found if one side and one angle are known — for example, the height of a 73-metre minar can be confirmed from ground level using the angle of elevation.

The procedure is to identify a physical situation involving a height, a base, and a line of sight, label the three sides of the resulting right triangle as opposite, adjacent, and hypotenuse relative to the angle of interest, and recognise that fixed ratios between these sides encode all measurable information about the angle. For example, in the Qutab Minar scenario, the ground from Priya to the base is the adjacent side, the minaret is the opposite side, and her line of sight is the hypotenuse, with her angle of elevation being angle A. This labelling convention is consistent throughout the chapter and is the prerequisite for defining trigonometric ratios in the next topic.

recall_questions.answer:
When the student stands on the ground looking up at the top of the Qutab Minar:
- The vertical height of the Minar = the side opposite to angle A (BC).
- The horizontal distance from the student to the base of the Minar = the side adjacent to angle A (AB).
- The student's line of sight to the top of the Minar = the hypotenuse (AC).
This is because the side 'opposite' faces the angle, the side 'adjacent' is part of the angle (not the hypotenuse), and the hypotenuse is the longest side, opposite the right angle.
recall_questions.prompt: For the Qutab Minar scenario, which physical feature represents the opposite side, which the adjacent side, and which the hypotenuse when angle A is the angle of elevation?

recall_questions.answer:
Given: vertical rise = 1 m (opposite to angle A), horizontal base = 3 m (adjacent to angle A), ramp surface = hypotenuse (AC).
Step 1: Identify the right angle — it is at the junction of the vertical rise and the horizontal base (the corner of the wall and the floor).
Step 2: Label the sides relative to angle A (the angle between the ramp and the ground):
  - Opposite (BC) = vertical rise = 1 m (the side that faces angle A).
  - Adjacent (AB) = horizontal base = 3 m (the side next to angle A that is not the hypotenuse).
  - Hypotenuse (AC) = ramp surface = √(1² + 3²) = √10 m (the longest side, facing the right angle).
Therefore the three sides are labelled: BC = 1 m (opposite), AB = 3 m (adjacent), AC = √10 m (hypotenuse).
recall_questions.prompt: A wheelchair ramp has a vertical rise of 1 m and a horizontal base of 3 m. Draw and label the right triangle formed. If angle A is the ramp's angle with the ground, state which side is opposite, which is adjacent, and which is the hypotenuse.

media.title: Aryabhata and the Origin of the Word Sine
media.description: A 110-second animated video tracing the historical journey of the word 'sine' and introducing the standard ratio notations. Screen 1 shows a title card: 'Aryabhata, A.D. 500'. Screen 2 displays a word chain in consecutive animated cards, each connected by a forward arrow: the word 'ardha-jya' appears in Devanagari script, transforms to 'jiva' (Sanskrit), then 'jiba' (Arabic), then 'sinus' (Latin), and finally 'sine' (English) — each transition animated as a card flip. Screen 3 shows Edmund Gunter (1581–1626) introduced with his name and dates; the abbreviation 'sin' appears in large text. Screen 4 presents all six notation cards — sin, cos, tan, cosec, sec, cot — appearing in sequence with their full names alongside, each in a distinct colour from the five-colour palette. Final screen shows the standard right triangle ABC with all six abbreviated ratio names placed next to the relevant side pairs. Text annotations only; no narration.
media.teaching_notes: Play AFTER students have read the six ratio definitions but BEFORE any numerical practice. Pause at 45 seconds — at the Arabic-to-Latin word step — and ask 'What do you notice about how the word changed as it moved between languages?' This activates the attempt-before-reveal effect for the historical story. Pause again at the final triangle screen (around 155 seconds) and ask 'Without looking at your notes, can you write sin A as a fraction of the triangle's sides?' to reinforce the notation convention before the answer appears.

Scene 1 (0–20s): Problem statement — a title card 'Aryabhata, A.D. 500' fades in on the centre of the screen in Navy Blue. On-screen annotation: 'The first use of the idea of sine in the way we use it today.' Scene 2 (20–60s): Setup — five word cards appear in sequence, left to right, connected by Orange arrows: 'ardha-jya' (Devanagari), 'jiva' (Sanskrit), 'jiba' (Arabic), 'sinus' (Latin), 'sine' (English). Each card animates in with a card-flip motion. Pause at 45s: text prompt 'Can you trace which language each word came from?' Scene 3 (60–90s): Edmund Gunter's name card appears; the abbreviation 'sin' is revealed in large Orange text beneath it. Then 'cos' appears below with 'Sir Jonas Moore, 1674'. WHY THIS STEP annotation: 'These abbreviations are still used today — they are not products of sin and A; they name a single ratio.' Scene 4 (90–140s): Six notation cards appear one at a time — sin A, cos A, tan A, cosec A, sec A, cot A — each paired with its full name: 'sine of angle A', 'cosine of angle A', etc. Each card uses a distinct colour. topics.topic_name: Defining the Six Trigonometric Ratios from a Right Triangle

topics.modified_chunk:
HOOK: We can see right triangles in staircases, ramps, and shadows — but seeing a triangle is not the same as measuring it. The question is: can we capture the shape of a triangle using numbers? That is exactly what trigonometric ratios do.

RECALL: In Section 8.1, you saw right triangles imagined to be formed in different situations. You also know from earlier classes how to calculate ratios. We now combine those two ideas — let us work through each definition carefully.

CORE — Setting Up the Triangle: Let us take a right triangle ABC as shown in Figure 8.4 in your textbook.

Here, angle CAB (or, in brief, angle A) is an acute angle. Note the position of the side BC with respect to angle A. It faces angle A. We call it the side opposite to angle A. AC is the hypotenuse of the right triangle and the side AB is a part of angle A. So, we call it the side adjacent to angle A.

Note that the position of sides changes when you consider angle C in place of angle A (see Figure 8.5). What was the opposite side for angle A may become the adjacent side for angle C — the labelling is always relative to the angle you are considering.

CORE — The Six Trigonometric Ratios: You have studied the concept of 'ratio' in your earlier classes. We now define certain ratios involving the sides of a right triangle, and call them trigonometric ratios.

The trigonometric ratios of angle A in right triangle ABC are defined as follows:

sine of angle A   =   side opposite to angle A / hypotenuse   =   BC / AC

cosine of angle A   =   side adjacent to angle A / hypotenuse   =   AB / AC

tangent of angle A   =   side opposite to angle A / side adjacent to angle A   =   BC / AB

cosecant of angle A   =   1 / sine of A   =   hypotenuse / side opposite to angle A   =   AC / BC

secant of angle A   =   1 / cosine of A   =   hypotenuse / side adjacent to angle A   =   AC / AB

cotangent of angle A   =   1 / tangent of A   =   side adjacent to angle A / side opposite to angle A   =   AB / BC

MULTIPLE REPRESENTATIONS — Three ways to remember these ratios:

Verbal form (read aloud): "Sine is opposite over hypotenuse; cosine is adjacent over hypotenuse; tangent is opposite over adjacent."

Ratio notation (abbreviated): sin A = BC/AC, cos A = AB/AC, tan A = BC/AB, cosec A = AC/BC, sec A = AC/AB, cot A = AB/BC.

Reciprocal relations (algebraic): cosec A = 1/sin A, sec A = 1/cos A, cot A = 1/tan A.

The ratios are abbreviated as sin A, cos A, tan A, cosec A, sec A, and cot A respectively. Note that the ratios cosec A, sec A, and cot A are respectively the reciprocals of the ratios sin A, cos A, and tan A.

Also observe the important derived relation:

tan A = BC/AB = (BC/AC) / (AB/AC) = sin A / cos A

and similarly: cot A = cos A / sin A.

These two relations — tan A = sin A/cos A and cot A = cos A/sin A — are used repeatedly in later work.

NOTATION CONVENTION: The six ratio names are written sin A, cos A, tan A, cosec A, sec A, cot A — always with a space between the function name and the angle label. We write sin²A to mean (sin A)², not sin(A²). These conventions are used consistently throughout this chapter.

So, the trigonometric ratios of an acute angle in a right triangle express the relationship between the angle and the length of its sides.

EXPLORATION PROMPT: Why don't you try to define the trigonometric ratios for angle C in the right triangle? (See Figure 8.5.) Which side is now opposite to angle C? Which side is adjacent? Write out all six ratios for angle C using the same format as above.

HISTORICAL NOTE — Aryabhata and the Origin of 'Sine': The first use of the idea of 'sine' in the way we use it today was in the work Aryabhatiyam by Aryabhata, in A.D. 500. Aryabhata used the word ardha-jya for the half-chord, which was shortened to jya or jiva in due course. When the Aryabhatiyam was translated into Arabic, the word jiva was retained as it is. The word jiva was translated into sinus, which means curve, when the Arabic version was translated into Latin. Soon the word sinus, also used as sine, became common in mathematical texts throughout Europe. An English Professor of astronomy Edmund Gunter (1581–1626) first used the abbreviated notation 'sin'.

The origin of the terms 'cosine' and 'tangent' was much later. The cosine function arose from the need to compute the sine of the complementary angle. Aryabhata called it kotijya. The name cosinus originated with Edmund Gunter. In 1674, the English Mathematician Sir Jonas Moore first used the abbreviated notation 'cos'.

ERROR ALERT — A Critical Point About Notation: The symbol sin A is used as an abbreviation for 'the sine of the angle A'. sin A is NOT the product of 'sin' and A. 'sin' separated from A has no meaning whatsoever. Similarly, cos A is not the product of 'cos' and A. Many students initially treat sin A like an algebraic product and try to 'cancel' the sin — this leads to completely incorrect results. The notation sin A is indivisible: it names a single number determined by the angle A. Similar interpretations apply to all other trigonometric ratios.

FURTHER NOTATION NOTE: We write sin²A as a shorthand for (sin A)², meaning the square of the number sin A. However, cosec A = (sin A)⁻¹, which is NOT the same as sin⁻¹A. The expression sin⁻¹A (sine inverse A) has a different meaning that will be discussed in higher classes.

CHECK: Given right triangle ABC right-angled at B, with BC = 3, AB = 4, AC = 5, write down all six trigonometric ratios for angle A. Then write all six ratios for angle C. Notice which values change and which stay the same.

8.2 Trigonometric Ratios

In Section 8.1, you have seen some right triangles imagined to be formed in different situations.

Let us take a right triangle ABC as shown in Fig. 8.4.

Here, ∠ CAB (or, in brief, angle A) is an acute angle. Note the position of the side BC with respect to angle A. It faces ∠ A. We call it the side opposite to angle A. AC is the hypotenuse of the right triangle and the side AB is a part of ∠ A. So, we call it the side adjacent to angle A.

Note that the position of sides change when you consider angle C in place of A (see Fig. 8.5).

You have studied the concept of 'ratio' in your earlier classes. We now define certain ratios involving the sides of a right triangle, and call them trigonometric ratios.

The trigonometric ratios of the angle A in right triangle ABC (see Fig. 8.4) are defined as follows :

sine of ∠ A = side opposite to angle A / hypotenuse = BC / AC

cosine of ∠ A = side adjacent to angle A / hypotenuse = AB / AC

tangent of ∠ A = side opposite to angle A / side adjacent to angle A = BC / AB

cosecant of ∠ A = 1 / sine of A = hypotenuse / side opposite to angle A = AC / BC

secant of ∠ A = 1 / cosine of A = hypotenuse / side adjacent to angle A = AC / AB

cotangent of ∠ A = 1 / tangent of A = side adjacent to angle A / side opposite to angle A = AB / BC

The ratios defined above are abbreviated as sin A, cos A, tan A, cosec A, sec A and cot A respectively. Note that the ratios cosec A, sec A and cot A are respectively, the reciprocals of the ratios sin A, cos A and tan A.

Also, observe that tan A = BC/AB = (BC/AC) / (AB/AC) = sin A / cos A and cot A = cos A / sin A.

So, the trigonometric ratios of an acute angle in a right triangle express the relationship between the angle and the length of its sides.

Why don't you try to define the trigonometric ratios for angle C in the right triangle? (See Fig. 8.5)

The first use of the idea of 'sine' in the way we use it today was in the work Aryabhatiyam by Aryabhata, in A.D. 500. Aryabhata used the word ardha-jya for the half-chord, which was shortened to jya or jiva in due course. When the Aryabhatiyam was translated into Arabic, the word jiva was retained as it is. The word jiva was translated into sinus, which means curve, when the Arabic version was translated into Latin. Soon the word sinus, also used as sine, became common in mathematical texts throughout Europe. An English Professor of astronomy Edmund Gunter (1581–1626), first used the abbreviated notation 'sin'.

The origin of the terms 'cosine' and 'tangent' was much later. The cosine function arose from the need to compute the sine of the complementary angle. Aryabhatta called it kotijya. The name cosinus originated with Edmund Gunter. In 1674, the English Mathematician Sir Jonas Moore first used the abbreviated notation 'cos'.

Remark : Note that the symbol sin A is used as an abbreviation for 'the sine of the angle A'. sin A is not the product of 'sin' and A. 'sin' separated from A has no meaning. Similarly, cos A is not the product of 'cos' and A. Similar interpretations follow for other trigonometric ratios also.
concept_bullets: Sine is the ratio of the side opposite the angle to the hypotenuse — for example, in right triangle ABC right-angled at B with BC = 3 and AC = 5, sin A = 3/5.
Cosine is the ratio of the side adjacent the angle to the hypotenuse — for example, with AB = 4 and AC = 5, cos A = 4/5.
Tangent equals sine divided by cosine and equals opposite over adjacent — for example, tan A = BC/AB = 3/4 when BC = 3 and AB = 4.
The three reciprocal ratios cosec A, sec A, cot A invert sin A, cos A, tan A respectively — for example, cosec A = AC/BC = 5/3 when sin A = 3/5.
The symbol sin A denotes a single number (the sine of angle A), not a product — writing sin × A or cancelling 'sin' is a meaningless operation.

The key method is to first identify which side is opposite angle A (the side facing angle A, which is BC), which is adjacent (part of the angle, which is AB), and which is the hypotenuse (AC), then form the required ratio. The reciprocal relationship — cosec A = 1/sin A, sec A = 1/cos A, cot A = 1/tan A — and the derived relation tan A = sin A/cos A are established immediately. An important notation caution: sin A is not a product of 'sin' and A but an indivisible symbol representing a single number determined by angle A.

sin A = (side opposite to angle A) / hypotenuse = BC / AC.
cos A = (side adjacent to angle A) / hypotenuse = AB / AC.

recall_questions.answer: The error: the student incorrectly treats 'sin' as a number or variable that can be multiplied by A. In fact, sin A is a single indivisible symbol — it represents the number that is the sine of the angle A. 'sin' separated from A has no mathematical meaning. Therefore '2 sin A' means 'two times the sine of angle A' (i.e., 2 × sin A), which is NOT the same as sin 2A (the sine of the angle 2A). For example, at A = 30°: 2 sin 30° = 2 × (1/2) = 1, but sin 60° = √3/2 ≈ 0.866, so 2 sin A ≠ sin 2A in general. The notation sin A is an abbreviation for a specific numerical value determined by angle A.
recall_questions.prompt: A student wrote: 'sin A is the product of sin and A, so 2 sin A = sin 2A always.' Identify the error in this statement and explain the correct interpretation of the notation sin A.

topics.summary: The theorem states that the values of the trigonometric ratios of an angle do not vary with the lengths of the sides of the triangle, as long as the angle remains the same. The proof uses the AA similarity criterion: in the two triangles PAM and CAB sharing angle A, both right angles (at M and at B respectively), the triangles are similar by AA. Similar triangles have corresponding sides in proportion — AM/AB = AP/AC = MP/BC — so MP/AP = BC/AC, which is sin A, regardless of which triangle is used. The same argument extends to triangle QAN. The insight is that any right triangle containing angle A is similar to any other, so all ratio values are fixed by the angle alone, not by the scale.
topics.topic_name: Invariance of Trigonometric Ratios under Scaling
topics.brief_summary: The invariance of trigonometric ratios under scaling is proved using the AA similarity criterion, showing that sin A, cos A, and all other ratios depend only on angle A and not on the triangle's dimensions.
topics.modified_chunk:
Now, if we take a point P on the hypotenuse AC or a point Q on AC extended, of the right triangle ABC and draw PM perpendicular to AB and QN perpendicular to AB extended (see Figure 8.6), how will the trigonometric ratios of angle A in triangle PAM differ from those of angle A in triangle CAB or from those of angle A in triangle QAN? Let us work through a formal proof.

THEOREM STATEMENT:
The values of the trigonometric ratios of an angle do not vary with the lengths of the sides of the triangle, as long as the angle remains the same.

GIVEN:
Right triangle ABC, right-angled at B, with acute angle A at vertex A. Point P lies on hypotenuse AC, with PM drawn perpendicular to AB (so triangle PAM is right-angled at M). Point Q lies on AC extended, with QN drawn perpendicular to AB extended (so triangle QAN is right-angled at N).

TO PROVE:
MP / AP = BC / AC,  AM / AP = AB / AC,  MP / AM = BC / AB
(i.e., the trig ratios of angle A are the same in all three triangles).

PROOF STEPS:

(i) Establishing similarity of triangles PAM and CAB.

In triangle PAM and triangle CAB:
— Angle PAM = angle CAB = angle A (same angle).
— Angle PMA = angle CBA = 90° (PM ⊥ AB and angle B = 90°).

By the AA similarity criterion (Chapter 6), triangle PAM ~ triangle CAB.

WHY THIS STEP? Two shared angles are sufficient to establish similarity by the AA criterion. Once similarity is confirmed, corresponding sides are proportional — which is exactly what we need to compare the ratios.

(ii) Writing the proportional sides.

Since triangle PAM ~ triangle CAB:

AM / AB = AP / AC = MP / BC

(iii) Recovering the trigonometric ratios.

From this proportion:

MP / AP = BC / AC = sin A

AM / AP = AB / AC = cos A

MP / AM = BC / AB = tan A

The ratios computed from triangle PAM are identical to those from triangle CAB.

(iv) Triangle QAN.

By the same AA argument (angle A is common; angle QNA = 90°), triangle QAN ~ triangle CAB. Therefore the trig ratios of angle A in triangle QAN are also equal to those in triangle CAB.

CONCLUSION:
From our observations, it is now clear that the values of the trigonometric ratios of an angle do not vary with the lengths of the sides of the triangle, if the angle remains the same. Whether we use a smaller triangle (PAM) or a larger one (QAN), sin A, cos A, tan A, and all reciprocal ratios remain unchanged. □

NOTATION NOTE: We write sin²A, cos²A, etc., in place of (sin A)², (cos A)², etc. Note that cosec A = (sin A)⁻¹ ≠ sin⁻¹A; the latter has a different meaning to be studied in higher classes. The Greek letter θ (theta) is also used to denote an angle — θ and angle A are interchangeable throughout this chapter.

ERROR ALERT: Two right triangles sharing angle A are similar, not necessarily congruent. The theorem establishes that corresponding side ratios are equal — not that the sides themselves are equal.

CHECK: If you double all sides of right triangle ABC to get a new triangle with sides 2AB, 2BC, 2AC, show that sin A is unchanged. What property of trigonometric ratios does this confirm?
topics.original_chunk:
Now, if we take a point P on the hypotenuse AC or a point Q on AC extended, of the right triangle ABC and draw PM perpendicular to AB and QN perpendicular to AB extended (see Fig. 8.6), how will the trigonometric ratios of ∠ A in △ PAM differ from those of ∠ A in △ CAB or from those of ∠ A in △ QAN?

To answer this, first look at these triangles. Is △ PAM similar to △ CAB? From Chapter 6, recall the AA similarity criterion. Using the criterion, you will see that the triangles PAM and CAB are similar. Therefore, by the property of similar triangles, the corresponding sides of the triangles are proportional.

So, we have

AM / AB = AP / AC = MP / BC

From this, we find

MP / AP = BC / AC = sin A.

Similarly,

AM / AP = AB / AC = cos A, MP / AM = BC / AB = tan A and so on.

This shows that the trigonometric ratios of angle A in △ PAM not differ from those of angle A in △ CAB.

In the same way, you should check that the value of sin A (and also of other trigonometric ratios) remains the same in △ QAN also.

From our observations, it is now clear that the values of the trigonometric ratios of an angle do not vary with the lengths of the sides of the triangle, if the angle remains the same.

Note : For the sake of convenience, we may write sin²A, cos²A, etc., in place of (sin A)², (cos A)², etc., respectively. But cosec A = (sin A)⁻¹ ≠ sin⁻¹ A (it is called sine inverse A). sin⁻¹ A has a different meaning, which will be discussed in higher classes. Similar conventions hold for the other trigonometric ratios as well. Sometimes, the Greek letter θ (theta) is also used to denote an angle.
concept_bullets: Two right triangles sharing an acute angle A are similar by the AA criterion — for example, triangles PAM and CAB both have angle A and a right angle, so they are similar regardless of their sizes.

Because corresponding sides of similar triangles are proportional, the ratio MP/AP (= sin A in triangle PAM) equals BC/AC (= sin A in triangle CAB) — the ratio value is unchanged when the triangle scales.

The invariance result means you may use any convenient right triangle to compute trigonometric ratios — for example, choosing a triangle with legs of length 1 and 1 for 45° gives the same sin 45° as any other isosceles right triangle.
The notation sin²A means (sin A)², the square of the sine of angle A, NOT the sine of A² — this convention applies uniformly to all six ratios.
topics.detailed_summary: The theorem states that the values of the trigonometric ratios of an angle do not vary with the lengths of the sides of the triangle, as long as the angle remains the same. The proof uses the AA similarity criterion: in the two triangles PAM and CAB sharing angle A, both right angles (at M and at B respectively), the triangles are similar by AA. Similar triangles have corresponding sides in proportion — AM/AB = AP/AC = MP/BC — so MP/AP = BC/AC, which is sin A, regardless of which triangle is used. The same argument extends to triangle QAN. The insight is that any right triangle containing angle A is similar to any other, so all ratio values are fixed by the angle alone, not by the scale.
important_points: the values of the trigonometric ratios of an angle do not vary with the lengths of the sides of the triangle, if the angle remains the same
AM / AB = AP / AC = MP / BC
MP / AP = BC / AC = sin A.
Note : For the sake of convenience, we may write sin²A, cos²A, etc., in place of (sin A)², (cos A)², etc., respectively.

recall_questions.answer: Any two right triangles that contain the same acute angle A are similar by the AA similarity criterion: they share angle A and both have a 90° angle, so two pairs of angles match. By the property of similar triangles, corresponding sides are in proportion. This means MP/AP = BC/AC (where triangle PAM and triangle CAB are the two similar triangles). Since MP/AP = sin A in the smaller triangle and BC/AC = sin A in the larger triangle, both ratios are equal — so sin A has the same value in both triangles. Because the ratio depends only on the angle A (not on the lengths of the sides), every right triangle containing angle A gives the same sin A.
recall_questions.prompt: Explain why the value of sin A remains the same in all right triangles that contain angle A, regardless of the size of the triangle.

recall_questions.answer:
Original triangle: sin A = BC/AC = 4/5.
New (doubled) triangle: sin A = 8/10 = 4/5.
Both values are equal: sin A = 4/5 in both cases.
This confirms the invariance of trigonometric ratios under scaling: the value of sin A depends only on the angle A, not on the size (scale) of the right triangle. When all sides are multiplied by the same factor, the ratios remain unchanged because the factor cancels in the numerator and denominator.
recall_questions.prompt: Right triangle ABC has BC = 4 cm, AB = 3 cm, AC = 5 cm. A student doubles all sides to BC = 8 cm, AB = 6 cm, AC = 10 cm. Compute sin A for both and state what property of trigonometric ratios this confirms.

recall_questions.answer:
AA Similarity Criterion: Two triangles are similar if two pairs of corresponding angles are equal.
Proof that triangle PAM ~ triangle CAB:
- Angle PAM = Angle CAB = Angle A (same angle, shared by both triangles).
- Angle PMA = Angle CBA = 90° (PM is perpendicular to AB; angle B = 90°).
Since two pairs of angles are equal, by the AA criterion, triangle PAM ~ triangle CAB.
Conclusion: Because the triangles are similar, corresponding sides are proportional — AM/AB = AP/AC = MP/BC — confirming that the trig ratios of angle A are the same in both triangles.

segments.summary: This segment builds the skill of representing any angle-and-distance problem as a labelled right triangle and reading off its trigonometric ratios. Starting with three motivating scenarios — the Qutab Minar, a river-bank view, and a hot-air balloon — it establishes why right triangles are the natural model for such problems and introduces the labels opposite, adjacent, and hypotenuse relative to a chosen angle. It then formally defines all six ratios for acute angle A in right triangle ABC and proves, using the AA similarity criterion, that these ratios are independent of the size of the triangle. Students learn to identify which side is opposite or adjacent for any given angle, compute all six ratios from side lengths, and justify the invariance result geometrically.

Step 2: Write six ratios for angle A.
sin A = 5/13,  cos A = 12/13,  tan A = 5/12,  cosec A = 13/5,  sec A = 13/12,  cot A = 12/5.

recall_questions.answer:
Proof sketch: Consider two right triangles PAM and CAB that both contain angle A at vertex A and have a 90° angle (at M and B respectively). Two pairs of angles match (angle A and the right angle), so by the AA criterion, triangle PAM ~ triangle CAB. By the property of similar triangles, corresponding sides are proportional: AM/AB = AP/AC = MP/BC. From this proportion, MP/AP = BC/AC, which is the definition of sin A in both triangles. Similarly, cos A and tan A are equal in both triangles.

opposite² = hypotenuse² – adjacent² = 75² – 60² = 5625 – 3600 = 2025.

topics.summary: When one trigonometric ratio is known for an acute angle, all five remaining ratios can be determined. The method is: (1) set the two sides implicated in the given ratio equal to multiples of a variable k; (2) apply the Pythagorean theorem to find the third side; (3) compute each of the other five ratios from their definitions. The key insight is that k cancels in every ratio, confirming that trigonometric ratios depend only on angle, not on size — so all six ratios encode pure shape information. For example, given tan A = 4/3, setting BC = 4k and AB = 3k gives AC = 5k by the 3-4-5 Pythagorean triple, and all six ratios follow immediately. A second worked example proves that equal sine values force two acute angles to be equal, using the SSS similarity theorem.
topics.topic_name: Finding All Six Ratios Given One Ratio
topics.brief_summary: All six trigonometric ratios are computed from a single given ratio by assigning sides using a variable k, applying the Pythagorean theorem to find the third side, and reading off each ratio from its definition.
topics.modified_chunk:
HOOK: We have defined six trigonometric ratios of an acute angle. A natural question now arises: if we know just one of these six ratios, can we determine all the others? Let us work through this carefully, step by step.

RECALL: From the definitions established in Topic T2, sin A = BC/AC, cos A = AB/AC, tan A = BC/AB, with the corresponding reciprocal definitions for cosec A, sec A, and cot A. From Topic T3, the actual lengths of the triangle's sides do not matter — only their ratios do. This means that if sin A = 1/3, we are not restricted to one specific triangle; any right triangle in which the opposite side is one-third of the hypotenuse will give sin A = 1/3.

CORE — Strategy: Given one ratio, use the ratio to assign values to two sides (using a scaling variable k), then apply the Pythagorean theorem to find the third side. Once all three sides are known, compute all six ratios directly from their definitions.

If in a right triangle ABC, sin A = 1/3, then this means that BC/AC = 1/3, i.e., the lengths of the sides BC and AC of the triangle ABC are in the ratio 1 : 3. So if BC is equal to k, then AC will be 3k, where k is any positive number. To determine other trigonometric ratios for angle A, we need to find the length of the third side AB. We will use the Pythagorean theorem.

AB² = AC² – BC² = (3k)² – (k)² = 9k² – k² = 8k²

Therefore, AB = 2√2 k.

(Why is AB not –2√2 k? Because AB is a length — a physical distance — and lengths are always positive. The negative root is discarded.)

Now, cos A = AB/AC = 2√2 k / 3k = 2√2 / 3.

Similarly, you can obtain the other trigonometric ratios of angle A using the definitions from T2.

ERROR ALERT: When sin A = 1/3, do not conclude that the triangle must have sides of lengths exactly 1 and 3. What you know is the ratio BC : AC = 1 : 3. The actual sides could be 1 and 3 (when k = 1), or 2 and 6 (when k = 2), or any other pair in that ratio. All such triangles are similar to one another and all give exactly the same sin A = 1/3. Trigonometric ratios encode shape, not absolute size. A similar warning applies to Example 1 below: when tan A = 4/3, that tells you BC : AB = 4 : 3, not that BC = 4 and AB = 3 specifically.

Remark: Since the hypotenuse is the longest side in a right triangle, the value of sin A or cos A is always less than 1 (or, in particular, equal to 1 in boundary cases).

Let us work through the textbook examples with full scaffolding.

---

WORKED EXAMPLE 1 — Complete (tan A given, find all six ratios):

Example 1: Given tan A = 4/3, find the other trigonometric ratios of angle A.

Step 1: Assign sides using the given ratio.

We know tan A = BC / AB = 4/3. So let BC = 4k and AB = 3k, where k is a positive number.

WHY THIS STEP? We introduce k to acknowledge that only the ratio is fixed, not the actual lengths. Any positive value of k gives a valid right triangle with tan A = 4/3.

Step 2: Find the hypotenuse using the Pythagorean theorem.

AC² = AB² + BC² = (3k)² + (4k)² = 9k² + 16k² = 25k²

Therefore, AC = 5k.

WHY THIS STEP? Once we have the ratio of two sides, the Pythagorean theorem gives us the third side. This is the standard mechanism for recovering all sides from one ratio — we always need all three sides before we can write all six ratios.

Step 3: Write all six trigonometric ratios.

sin A = BC / AC = 4k / 5k = 4/5

cos A = AB / AC = 3k / 5k = 3/5

tan A = 4/3   (given)

cot A = 1 / tan A = 3/4

cosec A = 1 / sin A = 5/4

sec A = 1 / cos A = 5/3

Notice that k cancels completely in every ratio — this confirms that the ratios are independent of the actual side lengths.

---

WORKED EXAMPLE 2 — Complete (equal sines imply equal angles):

Example 2: If angle B and angle Q are acute angles such that sin B = sin Q, then prove that angle B = angle Q.

Step 1: Set up the two right triangles.

Let us consider two right triangles ABC and PQR where sin B = sin Q. We have sin B = AC / AB and sin Q = PR / PQ. Then AC / AB = PR / PQ.

Step 2: Show all three pairs of sides are proportional.

Therefore, AC / PR = AB / PQ = k, say.   (1)

Now, using the Pythagorean theorem:

BC = √(AB² – AC²)

and QR = √(PQ² – PR²)

So, BC / QR = √(AB² – AC²) / √(PQ² – PR²) = √(k²PQ² – k²PR²) / √(PQ² – PR²) = k√(PQ² – PR²) / √(PQ² – PR²) = k   (2)

From (1) and (2), we have:

AC / PR = AB / PQ = BC / QR

Step 3: Apply the triangle similarity theorem.

By Theorem 6.4 (SSS similarity), triangle ACB ~ triangle PRQ, and therefore angle B = angle Q.

WHY THIS STEP? When all three pairs of corresponding sides are in the same ratio, the triangles are similar by SSS similarity. Similar triangles have equal corresponding angles — so angle B and angle Q, being corresponding angles, must be equal.

---

WORKED EXAMPLE 3 — Last step left for you to complete (cos²θ + sin²θ):

Example 3: Consider triangle ACB, right-angled at C, in which AB = 29 units, BC = 21 units, and angle ABC = θ. Determine the values of (i) cos²θ + sin²θ,   (ii) cos²θ – sin²θ.

Step 1: Find the missing side using the Pythagorean theorem.

AC = √(AB² – BC²) = √((29)² – (21)²) = √((29 – 21)(29 + 21)) = √(8 × 50) = √400 = 20 units.

WHY THIS STEP? We are given two sides of the right triangle but need the third to compute the trig ratios. The Pythagorean theorem is the tool for finding a missing side when two sides are known.

Step 2: Write sin θ and cos θ.

sin θ = AC / AB = 20/29,   cos θ = BC / AB = 21/29.

Step 3: Compute the required expressions — your turn to complete:

(i) cos²θ + sin²θ = (21/29)² + (20/29)² = (441 + 400) / 841 = ?   [Compute this value.]

(ii) cos²θ – sin²θ = (21/29)² – (20/29)² = (441 – 400) / 841 = ?   [Express this as a simplified fraction.]

---

WORKED EXAMPLE 4 — Further faded (tan A = 1, verify 2 sin A cos A = 1):

Example 4: In right triangle ABC, right-angled at B, if tan A = 1, then verify that 2 sin A cos A = 1.

Step 1: Assign sides.

tan A = BC / AB = 1, so BC = AB. Let AB = BC = k, where k is a positive number.

Step 2: Find the hypotenuse.

AC = √(AB² + BC²) = √(k² + k²) = k√2.

Step 3: Now over to you — find sin A and cos A, then verify that 2 sin A cos A = 1.

[Hint: Use the side values AB = k, BC = k, AC = k√2 and the standard definitions sin A = BC/AC, cos A = AB/AC.]

---

WORKED EXAMPLE 5 — Further faded (find sin Q and cos Q given a relation between sides):

Example 5: In triangle OPQ, right-angled at P, OP = 7 cm and OQ – PQ = 1 cm. Determine the values of sin Q and cos Q.

Step 1: Set up the algebra.

We are told OQ – PQ = 1, so OQ = 1 + PQ.

Step 2: Apply the Pythagorean theorem.

OQ² = OP² + PQ²

i.e., (1 + PQ)² = OP² + PQ²   (Why? Because OQ = 1 + PQ.)

i.e., 1 + PQ² + 2PQ = OP² + PQ²

i.e., 1 + 2PQ = 7²   (Why? Because OP = 7 and the PQ² terms cancel.)

Step 3: Solve for PQ and OQ, then find the ratios — your turn to complete:

[From the equation 1 + 2PQ = 49, find PQ. Then find OQ. Then write sin Q = OP/OQ and cos Q = PQ/OQ.]

---

CHECK: Given that cos A = 2√2/3 (from the opening example where sin A = 1/3), verify by computing sin²A + cos²A that the result is 1. What does this suggest about a general relationship between sin A and cos A? We will prove this relationship formally in a later topic.
topics.original_chunk:
We have defined six trigonometric ratios of an acute angle. If we know any one of the ratios, can we obtain the other ratios? Let us see.

If in a right triangle ABC, sin A = 1/3, then this means that BC/AC = 1/3, i.e., the lengths of the sides BC and AC of the triangle ABC are in the ratio 1 : 3 (see Fig. 8.7). So if BC is equal to k, then AC will be 3k, where k is any positive number. To determine other trigonometric ratios for the angle A, we need to find the length of the third side AB. Do you remember the Pythagoras theorem? Let us use it to determine the required length AB.

AB² = AC² – BC² = (3k)² – (k)² = 8k² = (2√2 k)²

Therefore, AB = ± 2√2 k

So, we get AB = 2√2 k (Why is AB not – 2√2 k ?)

Now, cos A = AB / AC = 2√2 k / 3k = 2√2 / 3

Similarly, you can obtain the other trigonometric ratios of the angle A.

Remark : Since the hypotenuse is the longest side in a right triangle, the value of sin A or cos A is always less than 1 (or, in particular, equal to 1).

Let us consider some examples.

Example 1 : Given tan A = 4/3, find the other trigonometric ratios of the angle A.

Solution : Let us first draw a right △ ABC (see Fig 8.8).

Now, we know that tan A = BC / AB = 4/3.

Therefore, if BC = 4k, then AB = 3k, where k is a positive number.

Now, by using the Pythagoras Theorem, we have

AC² = AB² + BC² = (4k)² + (3k)² = 25k²

So, AC = 5k

Now, we can write all the trigonometric ratios using their definitions.

sin A = BC / AC = 4k / 5k = 4/5

cos A = AB / AC = 3k / 5k = 3/5

Therefore, cot A = 1/tan A = 3/4, cosec A = 1/sin A = 5/4 and sec A = 1/cos A = 5/3.

Example 2 : If ∠ B and ∠ Q are acute angles such that sin B = sin Q, then prove that ∠ B = ∠ Q.

Solution : Let us consider two right triangles ABC and PQR where sin B = sin Q (see Fig. 8.9).

We have sin B = AC / AB and sin Q = PR / PQ

Then AC / AB = PR / PQ

Therefore, AC / PR = AB / PQ = k, say   (1)

Now, using Pythagoras theorem,

BC = √(AB² – AC²)

and QR = √(PQ² – PR²)

So, BC / QR = √(AB² – AC²) / √(PQ² – PR²) = √(k²PQ² – k²PR²) / √(PQ² – PR²) = k√(PQ² – PR²) / √(PQ² – PR²) = k   (2)

From (1) and (2), we have

AC / PR = AB / PQ = BC / QR

Then, by using Theorem 6.4, △ ACB ~ △ PRQ and therefore, ∠ B = ∠ Q.

Example 3 : Consider △ ACB, right-angled at C, in which AB = 29 units, BC = 21 units and ∠ ABC = θ (see Fig. 8.10). Determine the values of
(i) cos²θ + sin²θ,
(ii) cos²θ – sin²θ

Solution : In △ ACB, we have

AC = √(AB² – BC²) = √((29)² – (21)²)
= √((29 – 21)(29 + 21)) = √((8)(50)) = √400 = 20 units

So, sin θ = AC / AB = 20/29, cos θ = BC / AB = 21/29.

Now, (i) cos²θ + sin²θ = (20/29)² + (21/29)² = (20² + 21²) / 29² = (400 + 441) / 841 = 1,

and (ii) cos²θ – sin²θ = (21/29)² – (20/29)² = (21 + 20)(21 – 20) / 29² = 41/841.

Example 4 : In a right triangle ABC, right-angled at B, if tan A = 1, then verify that 2 sin A cos A = 1.

Solution : In △ ABC, tan A = BC / AB = 1 (see Fig 8.11)

i.e., BC = AB

Let AB = BC = k, where k is a positive number.

Now, AC = √(AB² + BC²)
= √((k)² + (k)²) = k√2

Therefore, sin A = BC / AC = 1/√2 and cos A = AB / AC = 1/√2

So, 2 sin A cos A = 2(1/√2)(1/√2) = 1, which is the required value.

Example 5 : In △ OPQ, right-angled at P, OP = 7 cm and OQ – PQ = 1 cm (see Fig. 8.12). Determine the values of sin Q and cos Q.

Solution : In △ OPQ, we have

OQ² = OP² + PQ²

i.e., (1 + PQ)² = OP² + PQ²   (Why?)

i.e., 1 + PQ² + 2PQ = OP² + PQ²

i.e., 1 + 2PQ = 7²   (Why?)

i.e., PQ = 24 cm and OQ = 1 + PQ = 25 cm

So, sin Q = 7/25 and cos Q = 24/25.
concept_bullets: Given one trigonometric ratio, assign the two relevant sides as multiples of k — for example, tan A = 4/3 means BC = 4k and AB = 3k for any positive k.
Apply the Pythagorean theorem to find the hypotenuse — for example, AC² = (3k)² + (4k)² = 25k², so AC = 5k.
All six ratios are then computed directly from their definitions; k cancels in every ratio, confirming that only the angle determines the ratios, not the triangle's size.
If sin B = sin Q for two acute angles B and Q, then all three pairs of corresponding sides are proportional (by SSS similarity), so triangle ACB ~ triangle PRQ and therefore angle B = angle Q.
topics.detailed_summary: When one trigonometric ratio is known for an acute angle, all five remaining ratios can be determined. The method is: (1) set the two sides implicated in the given ratio equal to multiples of a variable k; (2) apply the Pythagorean theorem to find the third side; (3) compute each of the other five ratios from their definitions. The key insight is that k cancels in every ratio, confirming that trigonometric ratios depend only on angle, not on size — so all six ratios encode pure shape information. For example, given tan A = 4/3, setting BC = 4k and AB = 3k gives AC = 5k by the 3-4-5 Pythagorean triple, and all six ratios follow immediately. A second worked example proves that equal sine values force two acute angles to be equal, using the SSS similarity theorem.
important_points: sin A = BC / AC = 4k / 5k = 4/5
cos A = AB / AC = 3k / 5k = 3/5
Therefore, cot A = 1/tan A = 3/4, cosec A = 1/sin A = 5/4 and sec A = 1/cos A = 5/3.
So, sin Q = 7/25 and cos Q = 24/25.

recall_questions.answer: When tan A = 4/3, we know only the ratio BC : AB = 4 : 3, not the actual lengths. Any right triangle in which BC is 4 parts for every 3 parts of AB will have tan A = 4/3. Introducing k (setting BC = 4k and AB = 3k) acknowledges that infinitely many triangles satisfy this ratio — for any positive value of k. The variable k is then cancelled out when we write the trigonometric ratios, confirming that the ratios depend only on the angle, not on the actual size of the triangle (consistent with the invariance proved in Topic T3). Setting BC = 4 and AB = 3 would be one specific case (k = 1), but it incorrectly implies those are the only valid lengths.
recall_questions.prompt: Explain why we introduce a scaling variable k when given tan A = 4/3, rather than directly setting BC = 4 and AB = 3.

recall_questions.answer:
Given: sin A = BC/AC = 3/5.
Step 1: Assign sides. Let BC = 3k and AC = 5k.
Step 2: Find AB using the Pythagorean theorem.
AB² = AC² - BC² = (5k)² - (3k)² = 25k² - 9k² = 16k²
Therefore AB = 4k.
Step 3: Write all six ratios.
sin A = BC/AC = 3k/5k = 3/5
cos A = AB/AC = 4k/5k = 4/5
tan A = BC/AB = 3k/4k = 3/4
cosec A = 1/sin A = 5/3
sec A = 1/cos A = 5/4
cot A = 1/tan A = 4/3
Note: k cancels in every ratio, confirming ratios are independent of triangle size.
recall_questions.prompt: Given sin A = 3/5, find all six trigonometric ratios of angle A. Show each step clearly.

recall_questions.answer:
The error: the student used absolute values (AC = 3, BC = 1) instead of introducing the scaling variable k. When sin A = 1/3, the relationship is BC/AC = 1/3, meaning BC and AC are in the ratio 1 : 3. Setting BC = k and AC = 3k (for some positive k):
AB² = AC² - BC² = (3k)² - (k)² = 9k² - k² = 8k²
Therefore AB = 2√2 k.
The student's numerical answer of AB = 2√2 happens to be correct only for k = 1 (i.e., BC = 1, AC = 3). The method is conceptually wrong because it fixes k = 1 without justification. The correct approach uses k throughout, and k cancels when the final ratios are written:
cos A = AB/AC = 2√2 k / 3k = 2√2/3.
recall_questions.prompt: A student was given sin A = 1/3 and computed AB as follows: 'AB² = AC² - BC² = 3² - 1² = 9 - 1 = 8, so AB = 2√2.' Find the error in this approach and show the correct working.

topics.summary: Exercise 8.1 spans three skill levels: computing all six ratios from given side lengths (Q1–Q2), recovering ratios from a single given ratio using the Pythagorean-theorem method (Q3–Q5), and justifying true/false claims about ratio properties (Q11). Q6 requires a similarity-based proof that equal cosines imply equal angles, paralleling Example 2 of Topic T4. Q7–Q10 require substituting computed ratios into composite expressions. The key procedural alert is that opposite and adjacent sides swap when the reference angle changes — what is adjacent to angle A is opposite to angle C — so labels must be reassigned before writing any ratio. The true/false items in Q11 test whether students can correctly identify that tan A is unbounded (not always less than 1), that sec A = 12/5 is achievable for some acute angle, and that sin θ = 4/3 is impossible.
topics.brief_summary: Exercise 8.1 provides structured practice in computing trigonometric ratios from given side lengths or ratio values, and in classifying statements about ratio ranges and notation as true or false.
topics.modified_chunk:
EXERCISE 8.1

Let us work through a strategy for each question group before you begin. STRATEGY: Q1–Q2 give specific side lengths — identify opposite, adjacent, hypotenuse, then apply definitions. Q3–Q5 give one ratio — assign sides using k, apply the Pythagorean theorem, then compute all ratios (Q4: isolate cot A from 15 cot A = 8 first). Q6 is a proof — adapt Example 2's similarity argument for cosine. Q7–Q8: find ratios, then substitute. Q9: use angle A + angle C = 90°, so sin C = cos A and cos C = sin A. Q10 mirrors Example 5. Q11: justify each true/false — recall sin θ ≤ 1 and tan A can exceed 1.

MODEL — Q1 (AB = 24 cm, BC = 7 cm, right angle at B): AC = √(576 + 49) = 25 cm. For angle A: sin A = 7/25, cos A = 24/25. For angle C: sin C = 24/25, cos C = 7/25. WHY FIND AC FIRST? All three sides are required before any ratio can be written.

1. In △ ABC, right-angled at B, AB = 24 cm, BC = 7 cm. Determine :
(i) sin A, cos A
(ii) sin C, cos C

2. In Fig. 8.13, find tan P – cot R.

3. If sin A = 3/4, calculate cos A and tan A.

4. Given 15 cot A = 8, find sin A and sec A.

5. Given sec θ = 13/12, calculate all other trigonometric ratios.

6. If ∠ A and ∠ B are acute angles such that cos A = cos B, then show that ∠ A = ∠ B.

7. If cot θ = 7/8, evaluate : (i) (1 + sin θ)(1 – sin θ) / (1 + cos θ)(1 – cos θ),  (ii) cot²θ

8. If 3 cot A = 4, check whether (1 – tan²A) / (1 + tan²A) = cos²A – sin²A or not.

9. In triangle ABC, right-angled at B, if tan A = 1/√3, find the value of:
(i) sin A cos C + cos A sin C
(ii) cos A cos C – sin A sin C

10. In △ PQR, right-angled at Q, PR + QR = 25 cm and PQ = 5 cm. Determine the values of sin P, cos P and tan P.

11. State whether the following are true or false. Justify your answer.
(i) The value of tan A is always less than 1.
(ii) sec A = 12/5 for some value of angle A.
(iii) cos A is the abbreviation used for the cosecant of angle A.
(iv) cot A is the product of cot and A.
(v) sin θ = 4/3 for some angle θ.

ERROR ALERT: 'Opposite' and 'adjacent' swap when you change the angle — the side adjacent to angle A is opposite to angle C. Re-label before every ratio you write.

CHECK: In Q7(i), expand each bracket as a difference of squares. What is the simplified form of the entire expression?

recall_questions.answer:
Step 1: Find AC (hypotenuse) first — it is needed for all ratios involving the hypotenuse.
AC = √(AB² + BC²) = √(24² + 7²) = √(576 + 49) = √625 = 25 cm.
Step 2: Compute sin A (opposite to A = BC; hypotenuse = AC).
sin A = BC/AC = 7/25.
Step 3: Compute cos C (adjacent to C = BC; hypotenuse = AC).
cos C = BC/AC = 7/25.
Note: sin A = cos C because A and C are complementary angles in a right triangle (A + C = 90°).
recall_questions.prompt: In triangle ABC right-angled at B, with AB = 24 cm and BC = 7 cm, find sin A and cos C. Show your working, stating which side must be found first and why.

recall_questions.answer:
False. tan A = BC/AB (opposite over adjacent). tan A < 1 only when BC < AB, i.e., when angle A is less than 45°. When angle A = 45°, tan A = 1. When angle A > 45°, BC > AB and tan A > 1.
Numerical example: Let BC = 4 cm, AB = 3 cm (a 3-4-5 right triangle). Then tan A = 4/3 ≈ 1.33 > 1. So for this acute angle A (where A ≈ 53°), tan A exceeds 1. The statement is false — tan A can take any positive value for acute angles.
recall_questions.prompt: State whether the following is true or false, and justify with a specific numerical example: 'The value of tan A is always less than 1 for any acute angle A.'

recall_questions.answer:
Step 1: Find cot A from the given equation.
15 cot A = 8 → cot A = 8/15.
Step 2: Since cot A = AB/BC = 8/15, let AB = 8k and BC = 15k.
Step 3: Find the hypotenuse using the Pythagorean theorem.
AC² = AB² + BC² = (8k)² + (15k)² = 64k² + 225k² = 289k²
Therefore AC = 17k.
Step 4: Compute sin A and sec A.
sin A = BC/AC = 15k/17k = 15/17.
sec A = AC/AB = 17k/8k = 17/8.
recall_questions.prompt: Given 15 cot A = 8, find sin A and sec A. Show all steps clearly.

segments.summary: This segment builds the skill of recovering a complete set of six trigonometric ratios when only one is given. Starting with a worked strategy — assign the two sides in the known ratio using a variable k, apply the Pythagorean theorem to find the third side, then read off all six ratios — it progresses through five increasingly faded worked examples that cover tan A given, equal-sine angles, combined expressions, and a side-difference constraint. The practice set (Exercise 8.1) consolidates these skills across computation, proof, and true/false classification. Students learn that trigonometric ratios encode the shape of a right triangle, not its absolute size, so a single ratio uniquely determines all five others.

important_points: We have defined six trigonometric ratios of an acute angle. If we know any one of the ratios, can we obtain the other ratios?
sin A = BC / AC = 4k / 5k = 4/5
cos A = AB / AC = 3k / 5k = 3/5
Therefore, cot A = 1/tan A = 3/4, cosec A = 1/sin A = 5/4 and sec A = 1/cos A = 5/3.

Since the hypotenuse is the longest side in a right triangle, the value of sin A or cos A is always less than 1 (or, in particular, equal to 1).

Given: sec θ = AC/AB = 13/12. Let AC = 13k and AB = 12k (k > 0).
WHY k: sec θ = 13/12 fixes only the ratio AC : AB = 13 : 12; actual lengths are unknown. The variable k represents the unknown scale.
Step 1: Find BC via Pythagorean theorem.
BC² = AC² – AB² = (13k)² – (12k)² = 169k² – 144k² = 25k².
BC = 5k.
Step 2: Write all six ratios (k cancels).
sin θ = BC/AC = 5k/13k = 5/13.
cos θ = AB/AC = 12k/13k = 12/13.
tan θ = BC/AB = 5k/12k = 5/12.
cosec θ = 1/sin θ = 13/5.
sec θ = 13/12 (given).
cot θ = 1/tan θ = 12/5.

recall_questions.answer:
Step 1: Find sin A and cos A from tan A = 1/√3.
Let BC = k and AB = √3 k. Then AC² = k² + 3k² = 4k², so AC = 2k.
sin A = BC/AC = k/2k = 1/2.  cos A = AB/AC = √3k/2k = √3/2.

Step 2: Since A + C = 90° (right triangle with right angle at B), sin C = cos A = √3/2 and cos C = sin A = 1/2.

Step 3: Compute each expression.
(i) sin A cos C + cos A sin C = (1/2)(1/2) + (√3/2)(√3/2) = 1/4 + 3/4 = 1.
(ii) cos A cos C – sin A sin C = (√3/2)(1/2) – (1/2)(√3/2) = √3/4 – √3/4 = 0.

modules.brief_summary: Trigonometric ratios are used to express the relationship between an acute angle and the sides of a right triangle, by defining six side-length ratios and proving they depend only on the angle.
modules.detailed_summary: Module 1 develops the foundational capability of computing all six trigonometric ratios — sin A, cos A, tan A, cosec A, sec A, and cot A — for any acute angle A in a right triangle. Starting with real-world scenarios (Qutab Minar, river bank, hot-air balloon), Segment M1.S1 establishes the context for why such ratios are needed, formally defines all six ratios as fractions of the sides of right triangle ABC, and proves using AA similarity that these ratios are invariant under scaling. Segment M1.S2 extends this toolkit by showing how to recover all six ratios from a single given ratio, using the Pythagorean theorem to determine the missing side. The unifying mathematical insight across both segments is that trigonometric ratios capture the shape of a right triangle — the angle alone determines all six numbers, independent of the triangle's size. This module lays the groundwork for Module 2, where exact ratio values are derived for the standard angles 0°, 30°, 45°, 60°, and 90°.
important_points: trigonometry is the study of relationships between the sides and angles of a triangle
sine of ∠ A = side opposite to angle A / hypotenuse = BC / AC
cosine of ∠ A = side adjacent to angle A / hypotenuse = AB / AC
tangent of ∠ A = side opposite to angle A / side adjacent to angle A = BC / AB
cosecant of ∠ A = 1 / sine of A = hypotenuse / side opposite to angle A = AC / BC
secant of ∠ A = 1 / cosine of A = hypotenuse / side adjacent to angle A = AC / AB
cotangent of ∠ A = 1 / tangent of A = side adjacent to angle A / side opposite to angle A = AB / BC
the ratios cosec A, sec A and cot A are respectively, the reciprocals of the ratios sin A, cos A and tan A
the values of the trigonometric ratios of an angle do not vary with the lengths of the sides of the triangle, if the angle remains the same
tan A = BC/AB = (BC/AC) / (AB/AC) = sin A / cos A
Since the hypotenuse is the longest side in a right triangle, the value of sin A or cos A is always less than 1 (or, in particular, equal to 1).

modules.summary: Module 2 develops the skill of working with specific numerical values of trigonometric ratios. Segment M2.S3 derives the exact values for all six standard angles — 45° from an isosceles right triangle, 30° and 60° from a bisected equilateral triangle, and 0° and 90° by a limiting argument — and collects them into Table 8.1. Worked examples then apply these values to find unknown sides and angles in right triangles, and Exercise 8.2 practises evaluating composite expressions and testing true/false statements about trigonometric behaviour. Segment M2.S4 shifts from computation to proof: the Pythagorean theorem is divided through by AC² to establish sin²A + cos²A = 1, the first Pythagorean identity, and this identity is immediately applied to express cos A, tan A, and sec A algebraically in terms of sin A. The unifying insight is that the Pythagorean theorem, once the ratios are defined, instantly generates algebraic identities that hold for every acute angle.

topics.summary: In a right triangle with one acute angle of 45°, the other acute angle must also be 45°, which forces the two legs to be equal. Setting each leg equal to a, the Pythagorean theorem gives hypotenuse = a√2. Substituting into the ratio definitions: sin 45° = a/(a√2) = 1/√2, cos 45° = a/(a√2) = 1/√2, and tan 45° = a/a = 1. The three reciprocal values follow immediately: cosec 45° = √2, sec 45° = √2, cot 45° = 1. A worked numerical check confirms that sin²45° + cos²45° = (1/√2)² + (1/√2)² = 1/2 + 1/2 = 1, previewing the Pythagorean identity. A notable consequence is that when the sun's elevation angle is 45°, the shadow of any vertical object equals the object's height, since tan 45° = 1.
topics.brief_summary: The values sin 45° = cos 45° = 1/√2 and tan 45° = 1 are derived from an isosceles right triangle with equal legs, by applying the Pythagorean theorem to find the hypotenuse and then reading off each ratio.
topics.modified_chunk:
HOOK: In Topic T4 you saw how knowing one trigonometric ratio lets you find all the others for any angle. Now a more fundamental question arises: what are the exact ratio values for the angles that appear most often in geometry and engineering — angles like 45°, 30°, and 60°? Let us work through the derivations carefully, because these values are the bedrock of all standard-angle calculations.

RECALL: From Topic T3, the values of sin A, cos A, tan A depend only on the angle A, not on the size of the triangle. This means we are free to choose any convenient right triangle — one with sides whose lengths we can calculate easily. For 45°, an isosceles right triangle is the most convenient choice.

CORE — The Geometry of 45°:

From geometry, you are already familiar with the construction of angles of 30°, 45°, 60° and 90°. In this section, we will find the values of the trigonometric ratios for these angles and, of course, for 0°.

In triangle ABC, right-angled at B, if one angle is 45°, then the other angle is also 45°, i.e., angle A = angle C = 45°.

WHY THIS STEP? The three angles of any triangle sum to 180°. If angle B = 90° and angle A = 45°, then angle C = 180° – 90° – 45° = 45°. The two acute angles are therefore equal.

Because angle A = angle C, the sides opposite these equal angles must also be equal:

So, BC = AB.

Now, suppose BC = AB = a.

Step 1: Find the hypotenuse using the Pythagorean theorem.

AC² = AB² + BC² = a² + a² = 2a²

Therefore, AC = a√2.

WHY THIS STEP? We chose the legs to both equal a so that the Pythagorean calculation stays clean. Any positive value of a gives the same ratios — confirming the invariance proved in Topic T3.

Step 2: Apply the definitions of trigonometric ratios.

Using the side labels established throughout this chapter — AB is adjacent to angle A, BC is opposite to angle A, and AC is the hypotenuse:

sin 45° = side opposite to angle 45° / hypotenuse = BC / AC = a / (a√2) = 1/√2

cos 45° = side adjacent to angle 45° / hypotenuse = AB / AC = a / (a√2) = 1/√2

tan 45° = side opposite to angle 45° / side adjacent to angle 45° = BC / AB = a / a = 1

Step 3: Compute the reciprocal ratios.

cosec 45° = 1 / sin 45° = √2

sec 45° = 1 / cos 45° = √2

cot 45° = 1 / tan 45° = 1

MULTIPLE REPRESENTATIONS:

Verbal: "At 45°, the opposite side and the adjacent side are always equal. The hypotenuse is √2 times either leg. Therefore the sine and cosine are equal — both equal 1/√2 — and the tangent is 1."

Numerical check: 1/√2 ≈ 0.707. Notice this is less than 1, which is consistent with the remark from Topic T4 that sin A and cos A are always at most 1 for acute angles.

ALTERNATE FORM: The value 1/√2 is often written with a rationalised denominator. Multiplying numerator and denominator by √2 gives 1/√2 = √2/2. Both forms are correct and appear in different textbooks.

CONNECTION TO REAL-WORLD CONTEXT: Recall from the example plan that Rajan observes a coconut tree casting shadows. When the sun's elevation is exactly 45°, the shadow length equals the tree's height — because tan 45° = 1 means the opposite and adjacent sides are equal. This is a direct application of the value we just derived.

ERROR ALERT: Many students rationalise incorrectly by writing sin 45° = 1/√2 and then concluding the denominator should be 2, writing 1/2. This is wrong. 1/√2 rationalises to √2/2, not 1/2. The denominator after rationalisation is 2 only in the final written form √2/2, but the numerator has become √2, not 1. A quick numerical check resolves this: √2/2 ≈ 1.414/2 ≈ 0.707 ✓, whereas 1/2 = 0.5 ✗. These are very different values.

CHECK: Using the six values just derived, verify that sin²45° + cos²45° = 1. Then verify that tan²45° + 1 = sec²45°. Do both identities hold? We will prove these identities hold for all angles in Section 8.4.
topics.original_chunk:
8.3 Trigonometric Ratios of Some Specific Angles

From geometry, you are already familiar with the construction of angles of 30°, 45°, 60° and 90°. In this section, we will find the values of the trigonometric ratios for these angles and, of course, for 0°.

Trigonometric Ratios of 45°

In △ ABC, right-angled at B, if one angle is 45°, then the other angle is also 45°, i.e., ∠ A = ∠ C = 45° (see Fig. 8.14).

So, BC = AB (Why?)

Now, Suppose BC = AB = a.

Then by Pythagoras Theorem, AC² = AB² + BC² = a² + a² = 2a²,

and, therefore, AC = a√2.

Using the definitions of the trigonometric ratios, we have :

sin 45° = side opposite to angle 45° / hypotenuse = BC / AC = a / (a√2) = 1/√2

cos 45° = side adjacent to angle 45° / hypotenuse = AB / AC = a / (a√2) = 1/√2

tan 45° = side opposite to angle 45° / side adjacent to angle 45° = BC / AB = a / a = 1

Also, cosec 45° = 1/sin 45° = √2, sec 45° = 1/cos 45° = √2, cot 45° = 1/tan 45° = 1.
concept_bullets: When both acute angles of a right triangle equal 45°, the two legs must be equal — setting both legs to a gives hypotenuse = a√2 by the Pythagorean theorem.
sin 45° = cos 45° = 1/√2 because the opposite and adjacent sides are equal; their common ratio to the hypotenuse is always 1/√2 regardless of the actual side length.
tan 45° = 1 because the opposite and adjacent sides are equal — for example, tan 45° = a/a = 1 for any positive a.
The rationalised form of 1/√2 is √2/2 (multiply numerator and denominator by √2); both are correct, but √2/2 is the rationalised denominator form.
topics.detailed_summary: In a right triangle with one acute angle of 45°, the other acute angle must also be 45°, which forces the two legs to be equal. Setting each leg equal to a, the Pythagorean theorem gives hypotenuse = a√2. Substituting into the ratio definitions: sin 45° = a/(a√2) = 1/√2, cos 45° = a/(a√2) = 1/√2, and tan 45° = a/a = 1. The three reciprocal values follow immediately: cosec 45° = √2, sec 45° = √2, cot 45° = 1. A worked numerical check confirms that sin²45° + cos²45° = (1/√2)² + (1/√2)² = 1/2 + 1/2 = 1, previewing the Pythagorean identity. A notable consequence is that when the sun's elevation angle is 45°, the shadow of any vertical object equals the object's height, since tan 45° = 1.
important_points: In △ ABC, right-angled at B, if one angle is 45°, then the other angle is also 45°, i.e., ∠ A = ∠ C = 45°
sin 45° = side opposite to angle 45° / hypotenuse = BC / AC = a / (a√2) = 1/√2
cos 45° = side adjacent to angle 45° / hypotenuse = AB / AC = a / (a√2) = 1/√2
tan 45° = side opposite to angle 45° / side adjacent to angle 45° = BC / AB = a / a = 1

recall_questions.answer:
Step 1: Construct the triangle. In right triangle ABC right-angled at B with angle A = 45°, the remaining angle C = 180° - 90° - 45° = 45°. Since A = C, the sides opposite them are equal: BC = AB. Let BC = AB = a.
Step 2: Find the hypotenuse.
AC² = AB² + BC² = a² + a² = 2a²
Therefore AC = a√2.
Step 3: Apply the definition of sine.
sin 45° = opposite/hypotenuse = BC/AC = a/(a√2) = 1/√2.
The value 1/√2 can also be written as √2/2.

cot 45° = 1/tan 45° = 1/1 = 1.

topics.modified_chunk:
HOOK: The isosceles right triangle gave us the 45° ratios neatly. For 30° and 60°, the starting point is just as elegant — an equilateral triangle, which is perhaps the most symmetrical triangle in all of geometry. Splitting it down the middle produces a right triangle whose sides are in an exact, clean ratio.

RECALL: In Topic T3 we proved that trig ratios depend only on the angle. In Topic T6 we chose a convenient triangle to derive the 45° values. We follow the same strategy now: choose the most convenient triangle, assign a manageable side length, then read off the ratios.

CORE — The Equilateral Triangle Construction:

Let us now calculate the trigonometric ratios of 30° and 60°. Consider an equilateral triangle ABC. Since each angle in an equilateral triangle is 60°, therefore, angle A = angle B = angle C = 60°.

Draw the perpendicular AD from A to the side BC.

Step 1: Establish congruence and symmetry.

Triangle ABD is congruent to triangle ACD. (Why? By the RHS congruence rule: angle ADB = angle ADC = 90°, AB = AC as sides of an equilateral triangle, and AD is common.)

Therefore, BD = DC and angle BAD = angle CAD.

Now observe that triangle ABD is a right triangle, right-angled at D, with angle BAD = 30° and angle ABD = 60°.

WHY THIS STEP? By bisecting the equilateral triangle, we create a right triangle in which every side length can be calculated exactly. The altitude AD bisects both the base and the top angle, turning a 60°-60°-60° equilateral triangle into a 30°-60°-90° right triangle.

Step 2: Assign side lengths.

As you know, for finding the trigonometric ratios, we need to know the lengths of the sides of the triangle. So, let us suppose that AB = 2a.

Then, BD = (1/2) BC = a   (since D bisects BC).

AD² = AB² – BD² = (2a)² – (a)² = 4a² – a² = 3a²

Therefore, AD = a√3.

WHY THIS STEP? Choosing AB = 2a keeps all calculations free of fractions. BD = a and AD = a√3 give a 30-60-90 triangle with sides in the ratio a : a√3 : 2a, which is the cleanest possible form.

Step 3: Derive ratios for 30° (angle BAD = 30°, with opposite = BD = a, adjacent = AD = a√3, hypotenuse = AB = 2a).

sin 30° = BD / AB = a / 2a = 1/2

cos 30° = AD / AB = a√3 / 2a = √3/2

tan 30° = BD / AD = a / (a√3) = 1/√3

cosec 30° = 1 / sin 30° = 2

sec 30° = 1 / cos 30° = 2/√3

cot 30° = 1 / tan 30° = √3

Step 4: Derive ratios for 60° (angle ABD = 60°, with opposite = AD = a√3, adjacent = BD = a, hypotenuse = AB = 2a).

sin 60° = AD / AB = a√3 / 2a = √3/2

cos 60° = BD / AB = a / 2a = 1/2

tan 60° = AD / BD = a√3 / a = √3

cosec 60° = 2/√3

sec 60° = 2

cot 60° = 1/√3

MULTIPLE REPRESENTATIONS:

Verbal pattern: "For 30°, the side opposite is the shorter leg (length a); for 60°, the side opposite is the longer leg (length a√3). Therefore sin 60° > sin 30°, which matches the general rule that sine increases as the angle increases from 0° to 90°."

Relationship between 30° and 60°: Notice that sin 30° = cos 60° = 1/2 and sin 60° = cos 30° = √3/2. This is not a coincidence. Since 30° + 60° = 90°, these two angles are complementary. The sine of an angle always equals the cosine of its complement, a result you can verify directly from the triangle.

CONNECTION TO EX3: Rajan observes a 10-metre coconut tree. At noon, the sun's elevation is 60°; the shadow length is the adjacent side relative to the 60° angle, so shadow length = 10 / tan 60° = 10/√3 ≈ 5.77 m. At 4 pm, the elevation is 30°; shadow length = 10 / tan 30° = 10√3 ≈ 17.3 m. The exact values derived above — tan 60° = √3 and tan 30° = 1/√3 — are what make this calculation possible without any calculator.

ERROR ALERT: A very common error is to write sin 30° = 1/√3 (confusing it with tan 30°). Here is how to check yourself: sin 30° should be less than sin 45° ≈ 0.707. We have 1/2 = 0.5 < 0.707 ✓. But 1/√3 ≈ 0.577, while tan 30° = 1/√3 ≈ 0.577 — the tangent, not the sine. The sine of 30° is exactly 1/2. A smaller angle has a smaller sine ratio: 30° < 45° < 60°, so sin 30° < sin 45° < sin 60°, which gives 1/2 < 1/√2 < √3/2 or approximately 0.5 < 0.71 < 0.87 ✓. Use this ordering as a sanity check whenever you recall these values.

CHECK: Using the values derived above, verify that sin²30° + cos²30° = 1. Then verify that sin²60° + cos²60° = 1. Both should hold. What does this suggest about the identity sin²A + cos²A = 1 across different angles?

recall_questions.answer:
When an equilateral triangle ABC (all sides = 2a, all angles = 60°) has its altitude AD drawn from vertex A to midpoint D of BC:
- Triangle ABD is right-angled at D (altitude bisects the base perpendicularly).
- Angle ABD = 60° (original equilateral triangle angle).
- Angle BAD = 30° (the altitude bisects the top 60° angle into two 30° angles).
- Sides: AB = 2a (hypotenuse), BD = a (half the base), AD = √(4a² - a²) = a√3 (altitude).
This is convenient because: (i) all three side lengths are exact and free of fractions when AB = 2a; (ii) a single geometric construction produces both 30° and 60° in one triangle; (iii) the invariance theorem (T3) guarantees any size gives the same ratios.
recall_questions.prompt: Describe how bisecting an equilateral triangle produces a 30-60-90 right triangle. Why is this the most convenient triangle for deriving the 30° and 60° ratios?

recall_questions.answer:
In right triangle ABD, angle ABD = 60° and angle BAD = 30°, with opposite = BD = a (for 30°), adjacent = AD = a√3 (for 30°), hypotenuse = AB = 2a.

For 30° (angle BAD = 30°; opposite = BD = a; adjacent = AD = a√3):
sin 30° = BD/AB = a/2a = 1/2.
cos 30° = AD/AB = a√3/2a = √3/2.

For 60° (angle ABD = 60°; opposite = AD = a√3; adjacent = BD = a):
tan 60° = AD/BD = a√3/a = √3.
cosec 60° = 1/sin 60° = 1/(a√3/2a) = 1/(√3/2) = 2/√3.
recall_questions.prompt: Using the 30-60-90 triangle with hypotenuse AB = 2a, shorter leg BD = a, and longer leg AD = a√3, find sin 30°, cos 30°, tan 60°, and cosec 60°. Show the working for each.

recall_questions.answer:
The error: the student confused tan 30° with sin 30°. In the 30-60-90 triangle with AB = 2a, BD = a, AD = a√3:
- sin 30° = opposite/hypotenuse = BD/AB = a/2a = 1/2 (NOT 1/√3).
- tan 30° = opposite/adjacent = BD/AD = a/(a√3) = 1/√3 (this is where 1/√3 appears — in the tangent, not the sine).
Sanity check: sin 30° = 1/2 = 0.5 < sin 45° ≈ 0.707 ✓ (since 30° < 45°, its sine should be smaller). But 1/√3 ≈ 0.577 > 0.5, so 1/√3 would incorrectly imply sin 30° > 1/2. The correct value is sin 30° = 1/2.
